explanations.explanation: That's the line, baker. Israel broke the yoke, tore off the chains and said, 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). A yoke is the heavy wooden bar that ties an ox to its work, so they were snapping loose from their load. I'd call that a big announcement for somebody about to go lie down under every green tree.

Not quite, friend. Nobody in this verse asks for a new king. The words are 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). They weren't shopping for a replacement. They were just done with serving, and they said it out loud while the chains were still hitting the ground.

Good guess, but land never comes up here. Israel broke the yoke, tore off the chains and said, 'I will not serve!' (Jeremiah 2:20). It's a cry about not serving, nothing about what they owned. Nobody was asking for a deed, just a door.

Right on it, baker. The LORD asks, 'How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?' (Jeremiah 2:21). He planted a choice vine from the very best seed. Best seed, best start, and the vine still went rotten. That's the sting in the question.

I see why you'd pick it, but that's not the picture. The LORD says they turned into 'a rotten, wild vine' (Jeremiah 2:21). Nothing about it being stripped. This vine grew wild, and it came out rotten after a choice start from the very best seed.

Roots never come up, friend. What the LORD says is 'a rotten, wild vine' (Jeremiah 2:21). He had planted them like a choice vine from the very best seed, so the contrast is the point. Great seed going in, rotten wild vine coming out.

Yes, stain. Even with lye and an abundance of soap, 'the stain of your guilt is still before Me' (Jeremiah 2:22). Lye is a harsh cleaner, so that's some serious scrubbing. And it still won't come out. No amount of elbow grease fixes that kind of mark.

Weight is a fair guess, since guilt does feel heavy. But the verse says 'stain,' and that's what soap is made to fight (Jeremiah 2:22). Washing with lye and an abundance of soap doesn't lighten anything. It just fails to lift the stain of guilt out.

Price makes sense in a bakery, baker, but not here. The word is 'stain' (Jeremiah 2:22). Soap is for stains, and that's the joke the LORD's picture is built on. They scrub with lye and plenty of soap, and the stain of guilt stays right there before Him.

Careful, friend, this one is the other way around. Israel doesn't admit it. The LORD quotes them asking, 'I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals' (Jeremiah 2:23). They're denying it. Then He says, 'Look at your behavior in the valley; acknowledge what you have done.'

That's right, baker. Israel denies it. They say, 'I am not defiled; I have not run after the Baals' (Jeremiah 2:23). The LORD answers by pointing at their behavior in the valley and telling them to acknowledge what they have done. Hard to say 'not me' when the evidence is that loud.

Close, but flip it. It's the opposite. The LORD says, 'All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her' (Jeremiah 2:24). Nobody has to chase hard, because she's easy to find. It's a rough picture of how eagerly Israel was running after other gods.

Yes, False. The LORD says, 'All who seek her need not weary themselves; in mating season they will find her' (Jeremiah 2:24). No long search needed. The picture is a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, sniffing the wind, and anybody looking for her knows right where she'll be.

Yep, that's their reason. They say, 'It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, and I must go after them' (Jeremiah 2:25). Notice they call it hopeless, but the reason is their own love for those gods. The LORD had just said they should keep their feet from going bare, and they said no thanks.

No kings in this excuse, baker. Israel says, 'It is hopeless! For I love foreign gods, and I must go after them' (Jeremiah 2:25). The reason comes straight from their own mouths, and it's about their own love. Nobody gets blamed but the loving.

Enemies don't show up in this verse, friend. The reason Israel gives is 'I love foreign gods, and I must go after them' (Jeremiah 2:25). It's not about being outmatched. It's about what they want and where they say they must go.

That's the word, baker. They say to a tree, 'You are my father,' and to a stone, 'You gave me birth' (Jeremiah 2:27). That includes their kings, officials, priests and prophets, the whole leadership. Calling a hunk of wood your dad. I've talked to a lot of dough, but I never asked it for an allowance.

Shepherd is a good Bible word, but it's not this verse. They say to a tree, 'You are my father' (Jeremiah 2:27). The stone gets 'You gave me birth,' so it's a family picture, not a flock one. Wood and rock standing in as parents.

Not king, friend. The tree is told, 'You are my father,' and the stone, 'You gave me birth' (Jeremiah 2:27). It's about who they say made them. Their own kings were in this crowd too, saying it right alongside everybody else.

explanations.answer: Let the gods they made save them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, 'But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can' (Jeremiah 2:28). They'd made those gods themselves, and now they were calling on them. Rise up and save yourselves, indeed.

explanations.answer: He is already on His way to them
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thought, but it's not what He says here. His answer is, 'But where are the gods you made for yourselves? Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can' (Jeremiah 2:28). He points them to the gods they'd made. They had turned their backs to Him and not their faces (Jeremiah 2:27).

explanations.answer: They should wait for Him at the temple
explanations.explanation: No temple waiting in this verse, friend. The LORD says, 'Let them rise up in your time of trouble and save you if they can' (Jeremiah 2:28). Them means the gods they made for themselves. He sends the cry right back to the gods they chose.

You got it, baker. The LORD asks, 'Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me' (Jeremiah 2:29). Walking into court to argue with Him while the whole group has rebelled. That's a bold way to start a lawsuit.

Not this time, friend. He says, 'Why do you bring a case against Me? You have all rebelled against Me' (Jeremiah 2:29). All of them. So the case they brought ran straight into what the LORD says about the rebelling.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, 'I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline' (Jeremiah 2:30). In vain means it didn't get through. I think that's the saddest part, because the correction came and nobody took it in.

If only, friend. The LORD says the opposite: 'I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline' (Jeremiah 2:30). Turning back would have made the striking worth something. Instead it was in vain.

No begging is mentioned here, baker. What the LORD says is, 'I have struck your sons in vain; they accepted no discipline' (Jeremiah 2:30). The discipline didn't take hold. Nothing in the verse says they asked for mercy.

Right, baker. The LORD quotes them: 'We are free to roam; we will come to You no more' (Jeremiah 2:31). He had just asked whether He'd been a wilderness to Israel or a land of dense darkness. Then He asks why His people would say that. A fair question.

Not quite, friend. The LORD asks, 'Why do My people say, "We are free to roam; we will come to You no more"?' (Jeremiah 2:31). That's what they say, and He asks them why. It's a real quote from His people, not something He made up.

That's it. 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). A bride doesn't forget her wedding sash, and yet they'd forgotten Him for that long. I'd bet nobody could count the days if they tried. I lose track of how long my cookies have been cooling, and even I'm not that bad.

Forty is a famous number in the Bible, but it's not this one. The LORD says, 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). Without number means too many to count. Forty would be a short stretch by comparison.

Seven years is a nice round number, baker, but the verse doesn't use it. The LORD says, 'My people have forgotten Me for days without number' (Jeremiah 2:32). No tidy count at all. Just days piled up past counting.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, 'you say, "I am innocent. Surely His anger will turn from me"' (Jeremiah 2:35). That's right after He mentions blood on their skirts and all these things. Then He says He will judge them because they say, 'I have not sinned.'

Other way around, friend. In spite of all these things, they say, 'I am innocent. Surely His anger will turn from me' (Jeremiah 2:35). They claim innocence, even with the blood of the innocent poor on their skirts (Jeremiah 2:34). That's what makes it so heavy.

That's the word, baker. 'Behold, I will judge you, because you say, "I have not sinned"' (Jeremiah 2:35). The reason is right there in the verse. They claim they haven't sinned, and He says He will judge them.

I understand the hope, friend, but the verse goes the other way. The LORD says, 'Behold, I will judge you, because you say, "I have not sinned"' (Jeremiah 2:35). Sparing would be a different sentence. This one names judgment and gives the reason.

Healing is a lovely word, but it isn't in this verse. The LORD says, 'Behold, I will judge you, because you say, "I have not sinned"' (Jeremiah 2:35). The word is judge. The reason is that they say they have not sinned.

Correct, baker. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Assyria was a mighty empire, and it let them down. Now they're looking to Egypt, and the same thing is coming. Same disappointment, new address.
I wish, friend, but no. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Just as. So Egypt lands in the same spot Assyria did. Nobody gets saved there.

explanations.answer: Egypt will defeat Assyria for them
explanations.explanation: That's a big plan, baker, but it isn't in the verse. The LORD says, 'You will be disappointed by Egypt just as you were by Assyria' (Jeremiah 2:36). Egypt doesn't ride in and win anything for them. It disappoints them, the same as Assyria did.

explanations.answer: With their hands on their heads
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. 'You will leave that place with your hands on your head' (Jeremiah 2:37). The reason given is that the LORD has rejected those they trust, so they won't prosper by their help. I think hands on the head is the picture of someone with nothing left to hold on to.

explanations.answer: With their arms full of gold
explanations.explanation: Wouldn't that be nice, friend. But no. The LORD says, 'You will leave that place with your hands on your head' (Jeremiah 2:37). Hands on head, not arms full. And He says they will not prosper by the help of those they trust.

explanations.answer: With a new army behind them
explanations.explanation: No army is coming, baker. The LORD says, 'You will leave that place with your hands on your head, for the LORD has rejected those you trust' (Jeremiah 2:37). The ones they trusted won't help them prosper. Hands on heads is how they walk out.

explanations.answer: Whether they would return to Him
explanations.explanation: That's the question, baker. 'But you have played the harlot with many lovers—and you would return to Me?' (Jeremiah 3:1). He begins with a picture of a man who divorces his wife and she marries another, asking if he can ever return to her. Then He turns it on them. It's a heavy question, and it's the LORD asking it.

Not this one, friend. The question is 'you would return to Me?' (Jeremiah 3:1). It's not about whether the lovers will stay. It's aimed at Israel coming back to the LORD after playing the harlot with many lovers.

explanations.answer: Whether Egypt will take them in
explanations.explanation: Egypt isn't mentioned in this verse, baker. After saying they've played the harlot with many lovers, the LORD asks, 'you would return to Me?' (Jeremiah 3:1). The question points back to Him, not to a place to go.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, 'You have defiled the land with your prostitution and wickedness. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and no spring rains have fallen' (Jeremiah 3:2-3). The word therefore connects the two. The reason is stated right there in the verse.

Good guess, but the verse names a different reason. The LORD says, 'You have defiled the land with your prostitution and wickedness. Therefore the showers have been withheld' (Jeremiah 3:2-3). Nothing about the priests going quiet. The land was defiled, and the rain stopped.

Treaties don't come up here, friend. The LORD says, 'You have defiled the land with your prostitution and wickedness. Therefore the showers have been withheld, and no spring rains have fallen' (Jeremiah 3:2-3). The reason is the defiled land, plain as that.

Yes, ashamed. The LORD says, 'you have the brazen look of a prostitute; you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). Earlier He said a thief is ashamed when caught (Jeremiah 2:26). Even a thief manages that much, and Israel won't.
Comforted sounds gentle, baker, but it's not the word. The LORD says, 'you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). The brazen look is the point. They had the look of someone who feels no shame at all.

Corrected is close in spirit, friend, but the verse says something else. The LORD says, 'you refuse to be ashamed' (Jeremiah 3:3). It's about shame, and they had none. Back in Jeremiah 2:30, the trouble was that they accepted no discipline, so you can see how those fit together.

I wish that were so, baker. But the LORD says, 'This you have spoken, but you keep doing all the evil you can' (Jeremiah 3:5). They asked the question and kept right on going. The words and the actions didn't match.

That's right, baker. After their words about His anger, the LORD says, 'This you have spoken, but you keep doing all the evil you can' (Jeremiah 3:5). They talk like a child calling out to a father, and then they keep doing it. The words were there, but the turning wasn't.
